Let the catalog sell, and let voice take the order: A storefront that suggests items works best for a kitchen buyer who has time to browse. A quick reorder at the end of a shift is a different moment. The two can work together.

Give each account the way in it prefers: Kitchens that are happy tapping through Choco's app can stay there. Offer the voice app to the ones who still call or text, which is where speaking the order helps most.
Orders land where they already land: Whatever you add, the order still arrives into the system you chose, or as an email to your desk. Nobody has to learn a new screen to receive it.

review.reviewBody: I used to spend hours every week ordering food. Now it's simple, super easy, and I have free time to spend on other aspects of my restaurant.

@graph.name: Short enough to finish this week
@graph.description: There is no data project to start, and nothing inside Choco changes. You send item lists, we set the customers up, and your customers begin sending orders.

step.name: Hand us the item lists
step.text: A spreadsheet is fine. Each account's items and your prices go into a single admin screen, lined up with your SKUs.

step.name: Your accounts get opened
step.text: We set up each account, and the customer downloads the app. Most have sent something in by the end of the day.

step.name: Your order arrives finished
step.text: The customer has approved it, and it carries a number and the time it was sent, in the format your system takes.

@graph.name: Do I need a Choco alternative to get voice ordering?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. You can keep Choco exactly as it is and add VoiceOrder Solutions next to it. Accounts keen to talk get our app; the ones happy in Choco's app stay put. Nothing has to be switched off first, and nothing in Choco has to change.

@graph.name: Would that make VoiceOrder Solutions a Choco competitor?

acceptedAnswer.text: Only in the narrow sense that both take orders. We do not run storefronts, sales tools or a CRM, and we do not want you to give those up. Most people who search for a Choco alternative want one thing added: an order the kitchen speaks and approves. They do not want a platform taken away.

@graph.name: Is VoiceOrder Solutions better than Choco?

acceptedAnswer.text: No, not at what Choco is built for: larger orders, tools for reps and customer records. We are stronger at one narrower job. The customer approves every item before it goes, so nobody at your end interprets a message. That is why we belong beside Choco, not in its place.

@graph.name: Does VoiceOrder Solutions connect to Choco?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The two are separate products, and each vendor supports only its own. Each one sends its own orders into your system. Ours come in the formats shown above, which your desk knows how to handle.

@graph.name: Won't some kitchens end up with two ordering apps?

acceptedAnswer.text: Only if you set it up that way, and mostly you should not. Leave the accounts that like Choco's app where they are and offer ours to the ones still on the phone. Calls keep coming to your desk as they do today, just without an order number from us, because only what is sent through our app gets one.

@graph.name: How soon can our accounts start?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most distributors are up and running within 24 to 48 hours, and most of their customers place a first order that same day. There is no IT project, and Choco carries on as normal throughout, so there is no switch-over date to plan around.

@graph.name: What does adding VoiceOrder Solutions cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: We quote each distributor separately and list no prices. Choco's own pricing page says it charges a monthly fee based on usage and asks you to talk to sales. Since you would be keeping Choco, the useful question is what the voice step adds on top, and a quote answers it.

@graph.name: Where do the Choco details on this page come from?

acceptedAnswer.text: Choco's own site, read on 10 October 2026: the module names and descriptions off the homepage and the usage-based line off their pricing page. We have not repeated the growth figures they publish, because those are their numbers and not ours to vouch for. If any of it has moved on since, this page is what needs correcting.
